title: Change one thing. Remember the rest.
alt: Three illustrative bicycle scenes: red frame at a wall, blue frame at the same wall, and blue bicycle in a new landscape.
caption: Teaching illustration, not FLUX output. Look for what should stay the same: basket, saddle, tires, and bicycle identity.
body: A text prompt can ask for a blue bicycle. A reference image asks for this particular bicycle in blue. Kontext has to learn both the requested change and the details that should survive.
takeaway: The reference supplies visual context. The instruction tells the model how to use it.
question: If the model makes a beautiful blue bicycle but changes its shape and removes the basket, did it succeed?
answer: Only partly. It followed the color request but failed to preserve the reference. Image quality, instruction following, and identity preservation are different questions.

title: Work on a compact representation.
alt: An image is encoded into an abstract, layered feature grid and then decoded into a reconstructed image.
caption: Conceptual autoencoder illustration. These colored tiles are not measured FLUX latent values, and individual tiles need not represent recognizable objects.
body: The autoencoder translates the image into a smaller spatial array of learned features. The flow model works on those features. A decoder turns the final features back into a visible image. Think of a compact working representation, not a folder of object labels.
takeaway: “Latent space” is where the numbers live while the image is being generated.
question: Does one latent channel mean one object, such as the bicycle or the wall?
answer: No. Channels are learned feature dimensions. The paper uses an autoencoder with 16 latent channels; it does not assign those channels to 16 named objects.

title: First, build an easy target to learn.
alt: A straight row from a clean bicycle image to noise, with training construction pointing toward noise and generation pointing back toward the clean image.
caption: Illustrative corruption sequence, not a numerical latent interpolation. The exact linear relationship is explored in the lab below.
body: During training we already know the desired output x. We draw random noise ε and pick a time t. Mixing the two gives zₜ = (1 − t)x + tε. For this one pair, changing t traces a straight line in latent space. Its velocity is especially easy to calculate: ε − x.
takeaway: A straight bridge gives us an exact direction to use as a training target.
question: Does the model know the clean target when someone requests a new edit?
answer: No. The clean target is available when constructing training examples. At generation time, the model has noise, the reference, and the instruction; it must predict how to move without seeing the desired answer.

title: Many straight examples teach one field.
alt: A straight line with consistent arrows for one training pair, next to a curved route following a spatially varying arrow field.
caption: Map analogy, not measured trajectories. The coral arrow follows a straight training bridge toward noise; the gold route travels toward the target. The lab below computes precise time-dependent directions.
body: The network sees many different image–noise pairs. It learns a rule: at this location, at this time, with this reference and instruction, which velocity should I predict? That rule is a velocity field. Following it can produce a curved trajectory even though the supervised examples used straight lines.
takeaway: Straight training paths do not promise straight generated paths or one-step generation.
question: If different training pairs pass through the same point at the same time, which arrow should a squared-error predictor learn?
answer: The conditional mean velocity: an average over the compatible examples, given the noisy target, time, reference, and instruction. The averaging experiment below illustrates this with two equally weighted examples.
source: §3, Eq. 3; Appendix A.1; squared-error interpretation derived for this guide

title: Keep the reference on the desk.
alt: Reference-image tokens, a text instruction, and noisy target tokens feed into attention; the evolving target becomes an output image.
caption: Information-flow metaphor, not an exact block diagram. The reference provides context throughout sampling; only the evolving target is generated.
body: Reference tokens are appended to the visual sequence. Attention lets the evolving target consult the reference and the instruction. The reference is not progressively turned into noise and cleaned again. It stays fixed as conditioning while the target changes.
takeaway: Two different roles: a fixed reference to consult, and an evolving target to construct.
question: Is the “1” in reference position (1, h, w) the same thing as flow time t = 1?
answer: No. The first positional coordinate identifies the image sequence. The flow time describes how far along the noise–data path the target is. They are separate inputs with separate jobs.

title: Better preservation still has limits.
alt: A ceramic mug changes over successive illustrative edits, gradually altering its handle, rim, and leaf emblem.
caption: Invented failure illustration. These are not paper samples or a measured degradation rate. The report’s real examples are in Figure 15.
body: An unwanted detail change can become part of the next reference image. Repeating that process can accumulate drift. Kontext improves consistency in the report’s comparisons, but it can still ignore instructions, change identity, or introduce artifacts.
takeaway: Check the intended change and what should have stayed unchanged.
question: Would returning the original image unchanged score well for identity preservation?
answer: It could—and still fail the edit completely. That is why a high face-similarity score alone is insufficient. Preservation and successful editing must be evaluated together.
